overviewHtml:
This graded quiz assesses your understanding of Husserl's phenomenological method and his analysis of intentional acts. You'll be asked about his critique of psychologism and account of givenness, the epoché, the phenomenological reduction, and eidetic variation, and the noetic and noematic structure of intentional acts.

Note: Aim for a score of 80 percent or higher. If you score lower, use the feedback to review the topics you missed, then retake the quiz.

forms.stemHtml: A philosopher claims that logic simply describes how evolution wired human reasoning. Which view is this?

options.html: Psychologism
options.text: Psychologism
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Grounding logical laws in facts about human psychology, here its evolutionary wiring, is psychologism.

options.html: Transcendental idealism
options.text: Transcendental idealism
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on psychologism and Husserl's arguments against it.

options.html: Eidetic science
options.text: Eidetic science
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on psychologism and Husserl's arguments against it.

options.html: The natural attitude
options.text: The natural attitude
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on psychologism and Husserl's arguments against it.

forms.stemHtml: A thousand students each judge that 7 + 5 \= 12. On Husserl's account, how many ideal contents are judged?

options.html: One ideal content, judged in a thousand acts
options.text: One ideal content, judged in a thousand acts
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! There are a thousand real acts, one in each student, but what is judged is one and the same ideal content.

options.html: A thousand ideal contents, one per student

options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on psychologism and Husserl's arguments against it.

options.html: Two ideal contents, one for each side of the sum
options.text: Two ideal contents, one for each side of the sum

options.html: No ideal content, only a thousand mental events
options.text: No ideal content, only a thousand mental events
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on psychologism and Husserl's arguments against it.

forms.stemHtml: You think of a friend's absent face, and then the friend walks in. What does Husserl call the experience of seeing the face you meant?

options.html: Disappointment of an empty intention
options.text: Disappointment of an empty intention
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on empty and fulfilled intentions.

options.html: Fulfillment of an empty intention
options.text: Fulfillment of an empty intention
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The face you meant emptily is now given in intuition, and you experience a coincidence between what was meant and what is given.

options.html: Suspension of the general thesis
options.text: Suspension of the general thesis
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on empty and fulfilled intentions.

options.html: Variation of an eidetic example
options.text: Variation of an eidetic example

forms.stemHtml: Which of the following describe the epoché? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: It suspends the belief that the world exists
options.text: It suspends the belief that the world exists
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The epoché puts the general thesis of the natural attitude out of action.

options.html: It puts the sciences' claims out of action
options.text: It puts the sciences' claims out of action
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! While the epoché is in force, no use is made of scientific claims, which rest on the general thesis.

options.html: It doubts whether the world really exists
options.text: It doubts whether the world really exists
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on the natural attitude and the epoché.

options.html: It denies that the world really exists
options.text: It denies that the world really exists
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on the natural attitude and the epoché.

forms.stemHtml: Complete the phrase: the general thesis belongs to the ________ attitude. Enter one word.

options.html: natural
options.text: natural
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The natural attitude is the ordinary stance in which the world is simply there, and the general thesis is its standing belief that the world exists.

forms.defaultFeedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on the natural attitude and the epoché.

forms.stemHtml: While performing the epoché on a cup, a researcher starts asking whether the cup is really there. What has gone wrong?

options.html: She has applied the epoché to the sciences as well
options.text: She has applied the epoché to the sciences as well
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on the natural attitude and the epoché.

options.html: She has slipped from suspending the belief into doubting it
options.text: She has slipped from suspending the belief into doubting it
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The epoché neither affirms, denies, nor doubts the world's existence. Asking whether the cup is real turns the method into Cartesian doubt.

options.html: She has moved from the epoché to eidetic variation
options.text: She has moved from the epoché to eidetic variation
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on the natural attitude and the epoché.

options.html: She has described the cup's givenness too carefully
options.text: She has described the cup's givenness too carefully
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on the natural attitude and the epoché.

forms.stemHtml: Judging that the train is late and asking whether the train is late differ in what respect?

options.html: They share an act matter but differ in act quality
options.text: They share an act matter but differ in act quality
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Both are directed at the train's being late, so they share a matter. Judging and asking are different kinds of act, so they differ in quality.

options.html: They share an act quality but differ in act matter
options.text: They share an act quality but differ in act matter
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on act quality, act matter, and adumbrations.

options.html: They differ in both act quality and act matter
options.text: They differ in both act quality and act matter
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on act quality, act matter, and adumbrations.

options.html: They share both act quality and act matter
options.text: They share both act quality and act matter
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on act quality, act matter, and adumbrations.

forms.stemHtml: When you perceive a tree, what is the noema of your perception?

options.html: Your act of perceiving the tree right now
options.text: Your act of perceiving the tree right now
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on noesis and noema.

options.html: A mental image of the tree in your mind
options.text: A mental image of the tree in your mind
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on noesis and noema.

options.html: The tree as perceived, from this side, in this light
options.text: The tree as perceived, from this side, in this light
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The noema is the object as meant, exactly as the act intends it. Here, that is the tree as perceived.

options.html: The light reflected from the tree to your eyes
options.text: The light reflected from the tree to your eyes
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on noesis and noema.

forms.stemHtml: Complete Husserl's term for givenness in which a thing is truly given but never exhaustively: ________ givenness. Enter one word.

options.html: inadequate
options.text: inadequate
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! A perceived physical thing is given through adumbrations, never completely, so its givenness is inadequate.

forms.defaultFeedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on act quality, act matter, and adumbrations.

forms.stemHtml: Which of the following are associated with the Fregean reading of the noema? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: Dagfinn Føllesdal's 1969 proposal
options.text: Dagfinn Føllesdal's 1969 proposal
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Føllesdal launched the Fregean reading, treating the noema as a generalization of Frege's Sinn.

options.html: Treating the noema as an intensional entity
options.text: Treating the noema as an intensional entity
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! On the Fregean reading, the noema is an abstract sense, not a physical thing or mental event.

options.html: Aron Gurwitsch's account of the perceptual noema
options.text: Aron Gurwitsch's account of the perceptual noema
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on the perceptual reading of the noema.

options.html: Treating the noema as the object considered as meant
options.text: Treating the noema as the object considered as meant
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on the perceptual reading of the noema.

forms.stemHtml: Husserl argues that logical laws can't be psychological laws. Which feature of logical laws supports this?

options.html: They're exact and known a priori, not vague and inductive
options.text: They're exact and known a priori, not vague and inductive
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Psychological laws are vague and empirical. Logical laws are exact and known independently of observation, so they can't be psychological laws.

options.html: They're learned by observing how people actually reason
options.text: They're learned by observing how people actually reason
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on psychologism and Husserl's arguments against it.

options.html: They hold roughly and admit many exceptions in practice
options.text: They hold roughly and admit many exceptions in practice
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on psychologism and Husserl's arguments against it.

options.html: They describe the typical workings of the human brain
options.text: They describe the typical workings of the human brain
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on psychologism and Husserl's arguments against it.

forms.stemHtml: On Husserl's account, which of the following is true or false?

options.html: The real act of judging, as an event in time
options.text: The real act of judging, as an event in time
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on psychologism and Husserl's arguments against it.

options.html: The causes that led a person to judge
options.text: The causes that led a person to judge
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on psychologism and Husserl's arguments against it.

options.html: The ideal content that is judged
options.text: The ideal content that is judged
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Truth and falsity belong to what is judged, the ideal content, not to the mental event of judging.

options.html: The feeling of certainty that accompanies a judgment
options.text: The feeling of certainty that accompanies a judgment
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on psychologism and Husserl's arguments against it.

forms.stemHtml: For Husserl, what is evidence?

options.html: A strong feeling of certainty added to a belief
options.text: A strong feeling of certainty added to a belief
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on empty and fulfilled intentions.

options.html: A statement that supports another statement logically
options.text: A statement that supports another statement logically
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on empty and fulfilled intentions.

options.html: A report of one's own inner mental states
options.text: A report of one's own inner mental states
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on empty and fulfilled intentions.

options.html: The experience of fulfillment, meant given as meant
options.text: The experience of fulfillment, meant given as meant
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Evidence is the experienced coincidence between an intention and the intuition that fulfills it. It comes in degrees.

forms.stemHtml: Which of the following are steps in free variation? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: Start from an actual or imagined example
options.text: Start from an actual or imagined example
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Free variation begins with an example of the kind in question.

options.html: Note which features can't be removed without changing the kind
options.text: Note which features can't be removed without changing the kind
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Features that survive every variation belong to the essence.

options.html: Count how often features appear across real cases
options.text: Count how often features appear across real cases
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on facts, essences, and free variation.

options.html: Suspend belief in the example's physical causes only
options.text: Suspend belief in the example's physical causes only
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on facts, essences, and free variation.

forms.stemHtml: What is the Greek-derived term for Husserl's suspension of the belief in the world's existence?

options.html: epoché
options.text: epoché
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The epoché suspends the general thesis without denying or doubting it.

options.html: epoche
options.text: epoche
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The epoché suspends the general thesis without denying or doubting it.

forms.defaultFeedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on the natural attitude and the epoché.

forms.stemHtml: Why did many of Husserl's early followers resist his transcendental idealism?

options.html: They thought the epoché was a form of doubt
options.text: They thought the epoché was a form of doubt

options.html: They read his earlier work as realist, and saw a relapse
options.text: They read his earlier work as realist, and saw a relapse

options.html: They thought phenomenology should rely on experiments
options.text: They thought phenomenology should rely on experiments
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on the phenomenological reduction and transcendental idealism.

options.html: They rejected the distinction between fact and essence
options.text: They rejected the distinction between fact and essence

forms.stemHtml: Two judgments are about the same building, one as "the tallest building in town" and one as "the old bank tower." How do they differ?

options.html: They differ in act quality but share act matter
options.text: They differ in act quality but share act matter
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on act quality, act matter, and adumbrations.

options.html: They share act quality but differ in act matter
options.text: They share act quality but differ in act matter
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Both are judgings, so they share a quality. They mean the building as different things, so they differ in matter.

options.html: They share both act quality and act matter
options.text: They share both act quality and act matter

options.html: They differ in both act quality and act matter
options.text: They differ in both act quality and act matter
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on act quality, act matter, and adumbrations.

forms.stemHtml: Which of these phrases describes a noematic sense?

options.html: "My act of remembering, which occurred this morning"
options.text: "My act of remembering, which occurred this morning"

options.html: "The station as seen from the platform, trains arriving"
options.text: "The station as seen from the platform, trains arriving"

options.html: "The neural activity that produced my perception"
options.text: "The neural activity that produced my perception"

options.html: "The sensations of color in my visual field"
options.text: "The sensations of color in my visual field"

forms.stemHtml: What is Husserl's term for the act side of an intentional experience, the meaning-giving act? Enter one word.

options.html: noesis
options.text: noesis
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The noesis is the act side. The noema is the object side.

forms.defaultFeedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on noesis and noema.

forms.stemHtml: Which of the following defend the perceptual, or object, reading of the noema? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: Robert Sokolowski
options.text: Robert Sokolowski

options.html: John Drummond
options.text: John Drummond
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Drummond treats the noema as the object as intended, not an intermediary.

options.html: Dagfinn Føllesdal
options.text: Dagfinn Føllesdal
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on the Fregean reading of the noema.

options.html: David Woodruff Smith and Ronald McIntyre
options.text: David Woodruff Smith and Ronald McIntyre
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on the Fregean reading of the noema.

forms.stemHtml: Why does Husserl say psychologism leads to a self-undermining relativism?

options.html: Because it holds that no human being can reason logically
options.text: Because it holds that no human being can reason logically
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on psychologism and Husserl's arguments against it.

options.html: Because it holds that logic is the same for every possible being
options.text: Because it holds that logic is the same for every possible being
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on psychologism and Husserl's arguments against it.

options.html: Because it makes truth relative to the species, yet claims this as true
options.text: Because it makes truth relative to the species, yet claims this as true
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! If logic depended on the human constitution, truth would be relative to the species. But the relativist puts that view forward as true, relying on the notion of truth it denies.

options.html: Because it treats every psychological theory as equally correct
options.text: Because it treats every psychological theory as equally correct
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on psychologism and Husserl's arguments against it.

forms.stemHtml: Frege's 1894 review of Husserl's Philosophy of Arithmetic charged Husserl with what error?

options.html: Treating numbers as physical objects in space
options.text: Treating numbers as physical objects in space
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on the Philosophy of Arithmetic and Frege's review.

options.html: Confusing subjective ideas with objective concepts
options.text: Confusing subjective ideas with objective concepts
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Frege charged that Husserl treated ideas in individual minds as if they were concepts and numbers, which are objective. For Frege, this was psychologism.

options.html: Ignoring the mental acts involved in counting
options.text: Ignoring the mental acts involved in counting
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on the Philosophy of Arithmetic and Frege's review.

options.html: Denying that arithmetic contains any truths
options.text: Denying that arithmetic contains any truths
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on the Philosophy of Arithmetic and Frege's review.

forms.stemHtml: What does the limit clause of the principle of all principles add?

options.html: Only scientific theories can override what intuition gives
options.text: Only scientific theories can override what intuition gives

options.html: What's given is accepted only within the limits it's given in
options.text: What's given is accepted only within the limits it's given in
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The limit clause restricts authority to what is actually given. A house seen from the front licenses claims about the front, not the back.

options.html: Introspective reports about one's states are never mistaken
options.text: Introspective reports about one's states are never mistaken
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on the principle of all principles.

options.html: Intuition gives objects only by way of mental images

forms.stemHtml: Varying the perception of a cup in imagination, which features turn out to be invariant? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: The cup is given from one side at a time
options.text: The cup is given from one side at a time

options.html: Hidden sides are co-intended as there
options.text: Hidden sides are co-intended as there
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! However you vary the example, some sides are hidden yet given as parts of the same thing.

options.html: The cup is a particular shade of white
options.text: The cup is a particular shade of white
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on facts, essences, and free variation.

options.html: The cup is made of glazed ceramic
options.text: The cup is made of glazed ceramic
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on facts, essences, and free variation.

forms.stemHtml: From the Latin reducere, "to lead back," what is the name of the phenomenological move that leads attention back to givenness? Enter one word.

options.html: reduction
options.text: reduction
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The phenomenological reduction leads attention back from objects, taken simply as existing, to their givenness in consciousness.

forms.defaultFeedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on the phenomenological reduction.

forms.stemHtml: Critics charge that eidetic variation is circular. What is the charge?

options.html: Variation needs so many cases that it never finishes
options.text: Variation needs so many cases that it never finishes

options.html: Varying "within the kind" needs a prior grasp of the kind
options.text: Varying "within the kind" needs a prior grasp of the kind
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! To know which variations keep the example the same kind, you seem to need some grasp of the kind already. Critics ask whether variation discovers essences or presupposes them.

options.html: Variation depends on doubting the example's existence
options.text: Variation depends on doubting the example's existence
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading comparing the three methods and critiques of eidetic variation.

options.html: Variation can be done only on objects that actually exist
options.text: Variation can be done only on objects that actually exist
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading comparing the three methods and critiques of eidetic variation.

options.html: Human eyesight is too limited to see objects clearly
options.text: Human eyesight is too limited to see objects clearly

options.text: Physical things change too quickly to be perceived

options.html: Perception gives only mental images of physical things

options.text: The noematic sense of each experience

options.text: The mode of belief in each experience

options.text: Phenomenology describes how objects appear, not contents
